newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Chinese navy plans running into trouble - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Chinese navy plans running into trouble - analyst.

text.p: China's ambitious plan to build a blue water navy beyond the turn of the century is running into formidable obstacles, an influential analyst said on Tuesday.
John Downing, the naval defence analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, told a naval conference in Singapore that Beijing wanted a blue water capability by 2020.
"China is probably only now beginning to understand the real problems that will have to be solved in order to achieve maritime domination," he said.
"The surface fleet will require considerable restructuring if it is to carry out its new tasks efficiently," he said.
Priorities for improvement included "air defence, command and control, combat intelligence, electronic warfare and logistic supply", he added.

Downing said China was still in the process of building a navy that could project serious force to any part of the region, the first stepping stone towards a blue-water navy which could do so in any part of the globe.
He said China had 1,100 naval ships, more than the United States, but most were for coastal defence.
Much work needed to be done to redress deficiencies in China's navy, ranging from ageing missiles to maintenance problems caused by the procurement of different systems, he said.

"The newest destroyer, the Luhu class for instance, must be a maintainer's nightmare, equipped as it is with Chinese-made 100 mm guns, French surface-to-air missiles, Italian torpedoes and American engines," Downing said.
The buildup of China's navy is taking place against a backdrop of disputes with other countries in the region.
They include wrangling over the Senkaku or Diaoyus islands with Japan and Taiwan.
Beijing is also locked in often acrimonious arguments over the Spratly islands with rival claimants Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and the Philippines.
